title: Counting Women in the Minyan
hookLine: women counted in the minyan and ordained as rabbis
carry: egalitarian: women counted in the minyan

cards: A weekday morning, early, in a small chapel. Prayer books are out, a few people are wrapped in prayer shawls, someone keeps checking the door.

Some prayers can only be said with a full quorum, a minyan, and they are waiting to begin. A woman sits in the second row. She knows every word of the service; she came to say the mourner's prayer for her father.
In some synagogues, she is the one who makes the quorum complete. In others, the room is still waiting. Same prayers, same morning, a different count.

teach.b: Egalitarian. It means equal, and in Jewish life it names a community where women and men take the same roles in prayer and leadership.
You met the minyan on day seventeen: a count of ten, so some prayers are never said alone. The Mishnah lists prayers not said with fewer than ten, and in traditional halakha those ten are men.
Women pray too, at home and in synagogue, but they were not counted, did not lead the public service, and were not ordained as rabbis. Then the change.
The Conservative movement's Law Committee took up the question in writing and approved counting women in the minyan. Later the movement's seminary began ordaining women as rabbis and cantors.
The Reform and Reconstructionist movements ordain women too.
But remember yesterday's rule: the committee can approve more than one answer, and the local rabbi chooses.
So Conservative and Masorti congregations went different ways: some became egalitarian, and some stayed with the traditional practice.
Orthodox communities keep the traditional minyan of men, and some have opened new roles for women within it, as you heard three days ago.

teach.h: MALE AND FEMALE CREATED HE THEM.
teach.b: Some who argued for the change pointed to the Torah's first chapter: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."
Those who held to the tradition answered from the long body of law on the minyan. Both sides argued from texts.
And for the woman in the second row, it's concrete: in an egalitarian room, when she walks in, someone at the door says, ten.

how: In egalitarian synagogues, women and men are counted equally in the minyan, are called to the Torah and lead services, and women serve as rabbis and cantors; other congregations keep the traditional practice.

games.q: you sit on the Conservative Law Committee. a woman who knows every prayer asks to be counted in the minyan. what do you rule?
o: she can pray, but not be counted.
games.why: the committee approved counting women in the minyan. as with every ruling, the local rabbi then chose, so some congregations became egalitarian and some did not.

practice: Think of a place you belong: a family table, a team, a congregation, a group of friends. Bring to mind one change in who was counted there, someone who moved from the edge to the middle, or the other way, and how it happened.
You don't have to judge it; just notice what it cost, and who carried it.

wordCard.voice: Egalitarian. A community where women and men take the same roles in prayer: counted in the minyan, leading services, ordained as rabbis. Today's word.
